Anatomy of a parabola

A quadratic graph forms a U-shaped curve called a parabola. Its key features help us understand its position, shape, and mathematical behavior.

plan.contextChunk: This figure graphs a single upward-opening parabola on a coordinate plane and annotates its main features with labeled arrows. Both axes are numbered from -6 to 6 over a dotted gray grid, with x labeled at the right end of the horizontal axis and y at the top of the vertical one. The curve is a heavy teal U with arrowheads on both rising branches; its lowest point sits at x equal to 1, y equal to -4, and the branches climb to about y equal to 5 near x equal to -2 on the left and x equal to 4 on the right. Small filled dots mark the two crossings of the x-axis at x equal to -1 and x equal to 3, the crossing of the y-axis at y equal to -3, the turning point, and the mirror partner of the y-intercept at x equal to 2. A red dashed vertical line runs through x equal to 1, reached by an arrow from the label Axis of symmetry above. Three further labels point to the graph and read x-intercepts, y-intercept, and Vertex. Drawing the dashed line through the turning point lets the reader check that the marked dots sit at equal heights on either side. The graph fixes the vocabulary for reading a quadratic.

interactionPlan.concept: A parabola's structure is governed by its vertex and axis of symmetry, which act as a rigid anchor and mirror line, while its intersections with the axes depend on its position and width.
elements: Cartesian coordinate plane with axes from -6 to 6, labeled at intervals of 2
Teal parabolic curve with arrowheads on both branches (initially y = (x-1)^2 - 4)
Red dashed vertical line representing the axis of symmetry (initially at x = 1)
Black dot at the lowest point with label 'Vertex' and pointing arrow
Black dot at the y-axis crossing with label 'y-intercept' and pointing arrow
Two black dots at the x-axis crossings with label 'x-intercepts' and pointing arrows
Black dot at (2, -3) acting as the mirrored pair to the y-intercept
Text label 'Axis of symmetry' with an arrow pointing to the red dashed line

interactions.label: Vertex x-position
interactions.teaches: Moving the vertex horizontally shifts the entire curve and perfectly translates the axis of symmetry along with it.

interactions.label: Vertex y-position
interactions.teaches: Moving the vertex vertically translates the turning point; raising it high enough can prevent the parabola from crossing the x-axis entirely.

interactions.label: Vertical stretch (a)
interactions.teaches: Changing the stretch factor alters how wide or narrow the parabola opens, which changes the distance between the x-intercepts without moving the vertex.

interactions.label: Highlight features
interactions.teaches: The vocabulary of a parabola categorizes into its central defining structure (vertex/symmetry) and its geometric intersections with the coordinate plane (intercepts).

demo_steps.title: Anatomy of a parabola
demo_steps.narration: A quadratic graph forms a U-shaped curve called a parabola. Its key features help us understand its position, shape, and mathematical behavior.

demo_steps.title: Vertex and Symmetry
demo_steps.narration: The vertex is the turning point. The axis of symmetry runs exactly through it, acting as a mirror—every point on the left has a matching partner on the right.

demo_steps.title: Moving the anchor
demo_steps.narration: If we shift the vertex horizontally, the axis of symmetry and the entire mirrored structure move in lockstep.

demo_steps.title: Intercepts and stretch
demo_steps.narration: The intercepts are where the curve crosses the grid's axes. Altering the parabola's width changes the distance between x-intercepts, and shifting it vertically can remove them entirely.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The vertex dictates the parabola's center and mirror line, while the stretch factor and y-position dictate if and where it crosses the x-axis.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Set up a standard 2D Cartesian grid from -6 to 6 with dotted lines. The main curve is a teal parabola (line width ~3px). Draw distinct solid black dots (radius ~4px) for the vertex, y-intercept, x-intercepts, and the y-intercept's mirror point across the symmetry axis. The axis of symmetry should be a prominent red dashed line. Connect the text labels to their points using thin black arrows. When the toggle switches, fade opacity of unselected dots and labels to 0.1 so the highlighted features stand out clearly.

authoredContext:
The graph of a quadratic function is a U-shaped curve called a parabola. One important feature of the graph is that it has an extreme point, called the vertex. If the parabola opens up, the vertex represents the lowest point on the graph, or the minimum value of the quadratic function. If the parabola opens down, the vertex represents the highest point on the graph, or the maximum value. In either case, the vertex is a turning point on the graph. The graph is also symmetric with a vertical line drawn through the vertex, called the axis of symmetry. These features are illustrated in the figure.

Graph of a parabola showing where the x and y intercepts, vertex, and axis of symmetry are.

The y-intercept is the point at which the parabola crosses the y-axis. The x-intercepts are the points at which the parabola crosses the x-axis. If they exist, the x-intercepts represent the zeros, or roots, of the quadratic function, the values of x at which y=0.

discrepancies: The 'Axis of symmetry' label is placed horizontally to the right of the dashed line, rather than above it with a downward-pointing arrow.
The arrows at the ends of the parabola are drawn as separate geometric arrowheads rather than smoothly integrating into the stroke of the curve.
The background grid lines are dashed rather than explicitly dotted.
The axes lack the distinct, short perpendicular tick marks seen in the source image (the generated chart relies entirely on the gridlines).
evaluation.notes: The generated figure accurately recreates the parabolic graph and its key anatomical features, offering excellent interactivity to explore how vertex position and vertical stretch affect the shape, though minor stylistic details like the grid pattern and arrow placements differ slightly from the source.

Add explicit, short tick marks crossing the main x and y axes to match the classic coordinate plane styling of the original figure.
